role: Tenant application developer on a multi-cluster Kubernetes platform (GitOps-only write path)
objective: Deploy a stateless web application from a git repo via GitOps. Objective: the minimum deploy path is documented and works.

l1.actor: Tenant application developer: an engineer on an onboarded tenant team with pull-request access to the platform repository. Supporting actor: the platform operator, who merges the PR and has granted repo access and (ad hoc) kubectl read access — per the docs, tenants have no self-service path for either.

preconditions.text: The tenant is onboarded: their engineers have write access (or a fork-and-PR flow) on the platform repository, and their changes are admitted by the platform's GitOps boundary (the platform-spoke ArgoCD project).

citations.heading: The onboarding procedure — Step 1
citations.quote: The tenant's engineers get write access (or a fork-and-PR flow) on the platform repository. All tenant delivery currently rides this repository.

citations.heading: What "onboarded" means
citations.quote: their application manifests are admitted by the platform's GitOps boundary

preconditions.text: A platform operator is available to merge the tenant's pull request; merge is the only deploy trigger.

citations.heading: Preconditions
citations.quote: You can open pull requests against the platform repository, and the platform operator merges them

preconditions.text: The application's container image is pullable from the cluster: a public registry, with a pinned tag.

citations.heading: Preconditions
citations.quote: Your container image is pullable from the cluster (public registry, pinned tag)

preconditions.text: The developer knows the target cluster's short name (e.g. platform), which becomes the hostname subdomain, and the platform's base domain <domain>.

citations.heading: Preconditions
citations.quote: You know which cluster you're deploying to — its short name (e.g. `platform`) is your hostname subdomain

citations.heading: What you need
citations.quote: The platform's domain, `<domain>` below — ask your operator, or read it off any existing platform URL.

preconditions.text: For verification, the developer (or the operator acting with them) has kubectl read access to the management cluster and to the application's cluster. NOTE: the docs name 'No human kubectl access path' as a product gap and the directory-group access guide is marked Stability: contract (not shipped), so this access is operator-granted out of band.

citations.heading: What you need
citations.quote: `kubectl` read access to the management cluster, and to the platform services cluster if you want to poke at runtime state.

citations.heading: Named gaps
citations.quote: No human `kubectl` access path

citations.heading: page header — stability marker
citations.quote: Stability: `contract`

steps.text: In a working copy of the platform repository, create a Helm chart for the stateless web app under platform-services/<your-app>/ containing Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/deployment.yaml, templates/service.yaml, and templates/ingress.yaml. In values.yaml, commit placeholder subdomain/domain values (the platform overrides them per cluster at sync time; never commit a real domain) and set the image repository plus a pinned tag.

citations.heading: 1. Add your chart
citations.quote: Create a Helm chart in the platform repository under `platform-services/<your-app>/`

citations.heading: 1. Add your chart (values.yaml)
citations.quote: Cluster facts — the ONLY platform values your chart receives. Committed values are placeholders; the platform overrides them per cluster at sync time. Never commit a real domain.

citations.heading: Step 1 — a chart for a tiny app
citations.quote: note the two placeholder lines; they are the platform's convention for 'filled in per cluster at deploy time'

steps.text: Write the Ingress template with ingressClassName nginx and a single-label host of the form <your-app>.{{ .Values.subdomain }}.{{ .Values.domain }} routing to the app's Service. Deliberately include no tls: block, no DNS annotation, and no certificate resource — DNS records and TLS are platform machinery (ExternalDNS creates the Route53 record from the rule host; TLS terminates at the cluster's ingress load balancer with the cluster's wildcard certificate).

citations.heading: 1. Add an Ingress to your chart
citations.quote: No `tls:` block. TLS terminates at the cluster's ingress load balancer with the cluster's wildcard certificate

citations.heading: 1. Add an Ingress to your chart
citations.quote: one label under the cluster subdomain (`myapp.platform.<domain>`, never `a.b.platform.<domain>`)

citations.heading: DNS records
citations.quote: Declaring an Ingress with `host: myapp.<subdomain>.<domain>` is sufficient — the record appears without any annotation.

steps.text: Create the deployment unit at argocd/apps/spoke/<your-app>.yaml: an ArgoCD ApplicationSet using the cluster generator with matchLabels k8-platform.io/cluster-role: spoke (it targets every registered spoke cluster), project platform-spoke, source repoURL = the platform repository with path platform-services/<your-app>, destination namespace <your-app>, automated sync with prune: true and selfHeal: true, and syncOptions CreateNamespace=true and ServerSideApply=true. The template injects the real domain/subdomain from each cluster's k8-platform.io/domain and k8-platform.io/subdomain annotations, and names each generated Application '<cluster-short-name>-<your-app>'.

citations.heading: 2. Add the Application file
citations.quote: clusters: selector: matchLabels: k8-platform.io/cluster-role: spoke

citations.heading: Step 2 — tell the platform to run it
citations.quote: This is the platform's deployment unit: it targets every registered spoke cluster and injects the real `domain`/`subdomain` into your values

citations.heading: 2. Add the Application file
citations.quote: '{{index .metadata.labels "k8-platform.io/short-name"}}-myapp'

steps.text: Open a single pull request containing both changes (the chart and the ApplicationSet file) and get the platform operator to merge it to main. Issue no deploy command — once merged, the platform's app-of-apps picks the new Application up automatically and the sync starts within minutes.

citations.heading: Step 2 — tell the platform to run it
citations.quote: Open the PR with both changes; get it merged.

citations.heading: 3. Commit and merge
citations.quote: Once merged to `main`, the platform's app-of-apps picks the new Application up automatically — no further action.

citations.heading: Step 3 — watch the platform do the rest
citations.quote: You issued no deploy command, and you won't.

steps.text: On the management cluster, within a few minutes of the merge, check delivery health: kubectl get application <cluster-short-name>-<your-app> -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.status.sync.status}/{.status.health.status}' and watch it move to Synced/Healthy. If it degrades, read .status.operationState.message for the reason.

citations.heading: Is it delivered? (Argo CD Application)
citations.quote: kubectl get application <cluster-short-name>-<app> -n argocd -o jsonpath='{.status.sync.status}/{.status.health.status}'

citations.heading: Step 3 — watch the platform do the rest
citations.quote: Watch it move to `Synced/Healthy`.

citations.heading: 3. Commit and merge
citations.quote: the sync starts within minutes and retries with backoff if a dependency isn't ready yet.

steps.text: On the cluster the app runs on, confirm runtime health in the app's namespace (created automatically on sync): kubectl -n <your-app> get pods and kubectl -n <your-app> rollout status deploy/<your-app>; if anything looks off, check recent events and logs.

citations.heading: 4. Verify
citations.quote: kubectl -n myapp get pods

citations.heading: What you can rely on
citations.quote: Namespace and ordering are handled: your namespace is created on sync

citations.heading: Is it running? (your namespace)
citations.quote: kubectl -n <ns> rollout status deploy/<name>

steps.text: Find the published URL from the Ingress rule host (kubectl -n <your-app> get ingress <your-app> -o jsonpath='{.spec.rules[0].host}'), allow a minute or two for first-time DNS (dig +short the host if curl fails), then request it with full certificate verification: curl -sSf https://<your-app>.<subdomain>.<domain>.

citations.heading: What's the URL, and does it answer?
citations.quote: kubectl -n <ns> get ingress <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.rules[0].host}'

citations.heading: Step 4 — visit your URL
citations.quote: First-time DNS can lag a minute or two — if `curl` fails, `dig +short hi.platform.<domain>` first.

citations.heading: 3. Verify
citations.quote: curl verifying the certificate without flags is the point: a self-signed or missing cert here is a platform defect.

observable_outcome.text: Without any deploy command being issued: (a) on the management cluster the ArgoCD Application <cluster-short-name>-<your-app> reports Synced/Healthy (Git and cluster agree, workload reports ready); (b) the namespace <your-app> exists on the spoke cluster with the Deployment's pods Running and the rollout complete; (c) a real DNS record and a valid public certificate exist for <your-app>.<subdomain>.<domain> although the tenant requested neither; and (d) curl -sSf https://<your-app>.<subdomain>.<domain> returns HTTP 200 over verified TLS — the platform's own definition of a working exposure. Once the Ingress is synced and healthy, NXDOMAIN or failing certificate verification is a platform defect, not an expected state.

citations.heading: What's the URL, and does it answer?
citations.quote: HTTP 200 over verified TLS is the platform's definition of a working exposure.

citations.heading: Step 4 — visit your URL
citations.quote: A real DNS record and a valid public certificate, and you asked for neither

citations.heading: What this means for a scenario oracle
citations.quote: A failing certificate verification or NXDOMAIN is a platform defect, not an expected state, once the application's Ingress is synced and healthy.

defect_classes: Docs-drift defects: the documented minimum path (file locations platform-services/<app>/ and argocd/apps/spoke/<app>.yaml, ApplicationSet fields, <short-name>-<app> naming) no longer matches what the platform actually accepts or generates.
GitOps pickup defects: a merged Application file under argocd/apps/spoke/ is never discovered by the hub's app-of-apps, or sync does not start within the documented 'minutes'.

Admission/boundary regressions: the platform-spoke project denies a permitted workload kind or the platform repository source (denial surface: 'resource <group>:<Kind> is not permitted in project platform-spoke' with SyncFailed/degraded status).

Cluster-fact injection defects: the k8-platform.io/domain / k8-platform.io/subdomain annotations are missing or not injected, so placeholder values leak into rendered manifests and the Ingress host is wrong.
Namespace automation defects: CreateNamespace=true not honored, so the first sync fails on a missing namespace.
DNS automation defects: ExternalDNS fails to create the Route53 record from the Ingress rule host (NXDOMAIN persisting beyond the documented couple of minutes after sync).
TLS defects: the cluster wildcard certificate is missing, self-signed, expired, or does not cover <app>.<subdomain>.<domain>, so curl's certificate verification fails.
Health-surface defects: the Application reports Synced/Healthy while pods are not ready (or stays OutOfSync/Degraded after a correct apply) — the status surface lies to the tenant.
Image-path defects: a public, pinned-tag image cannot be pulled from the spoke cluster (registry egress or image policy broken despite meeting the documented precondition).
Prune/self-heal symmetry defects: reverting the deploy commit does not undo the deployment (the documented 'no rollback command because there is no deploy command' model breaks).

Access-path defects: the tenant cannot execute the documented verification because no shipped kubectl access path exists for tenant humans — the scenario surfaces the doc/product mismatch between stable verification steps and contract-only access.

missing_facts: The normative identity/URL of 'the platform repository' a tenant must clone and PR against: it appears only as an example value inside the ApplicationSet YAML (repoURL: https://github.com/lago-morph/k8-platform.git) and is never stated as a fact anywhere ('the platform repository is at X'); note the repo is spelled k8-platform while the docs site is k8s-platform.

The process or channel for a tenant to request onboarding/PR access: onboarding says the operator grants write access and explicitly names 'No tenant self-service ... no request flow', but no contact point, ticketing path, or request procedure is documented.

A shipped way for a tenant human to obtain the kubectl read access every verification step depends on: 'No human kubectl access path' is a named gap, the directory-group guide is Stability: contract (explicitly 'not shipped yet'), and how operators grant interim access is undocumented.

How to obtain a kubeconfig/API endpoint for the management cluster specifically: even the contract-stage access guide covers only the platform services cluster, yet delivery-health verification (step 5) must run 'On the management cluster'.

How to discover which spoke clusters are registered and their short names/subdomains: the deploy precondition says 'You know which cluster you're deploying to', but no command or page enumerates registered spokes or their k8-platform.io/short-name / subdomain values ('ask your operator' is offered only for the domain).

How to deploy to exactly one chosen cluster: the documented ApplicationSet 'targets every registered spoke cluster' via the cluster-role: spoke selector, contradicting the single-cluster framing of the precondition; no documented selector or pattern pins an app to a single named spoke.
Whether private/authenticated container registries are supported and how to supply pull credentials: the precondition permits only 'public registry, pinned tag' with no documented alternative.

Whether tenant namespaces carry ResourceQuota, LimitRange, PodSecurity, or other admission constraints that could block a minimal Deployment: the tenant-boundaries reference covers ArgoCD project boundaries (kinds, sources, destinations) but says nothing about in-namespace runtime constraints.

How application/namespace name collisions between tenants are prevented: destination namespace equals the app name, tenants 'share the same project' (named gap: 'No per-tenant isolation between tenants'), and no uniqueness or reservation rule is documented beyond implicit PR review.

A bounded end-to-end latency for the deploy path usable as a scenario timeout: docs give only 'within a few minutes of the merge' for sync and 'a minute or two' / 'up to a couple of minutes' for first DNS, with no upper bound at which the run should be declared failed.
PR review/merge expectations: what the platform operator checks before merging a tenant PR and any turnaround expectation — 'the platform operator merges them' is the entire documented contract.

What the tenant's Deployment must expose for ArgoCD to call it Healthy (readiness probes, labels, service/port naming beyond the examples): health is defined only as 'resources report ready (Deployments available, etc.)'.

assumptions.statement: Standard git and GitHub pull-request mechanics (clone/fork, branch, commit, open PR, git revert via PR) work as in vanilla GitHub; the docs invoke them ('Open the PR', 'git revert HEAD # via a PR, like everything') without defining them.
Helm chart structure (Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/) and {{ .Values.* }} substitution behave per standard Helm v2 chart apiVersion semantics.

ArgoCD ApplicationSet cluster-generator semantics: matchLabels selects registered cluster secrets on the management cluster and renders one Application per matching cluster; automated prune+selfHeal keeps cluster state converged to Git.
curl -sSf performs full TLS verification against the system trust store and fails on an invalid/self-signed certificate, so an HTTP 200 from it implies a valid publicly-trusted certificate.
The platform repository is the GitHub repository shown in the example ApplicationSet (https://github.com/lago-morph/k8-platform.git); the docs never assert this outside example YAML.

Deploying to every registered spoke (the documented deployment unit) is acceptable as the minimum path, and in the reference build the app answers at the 'platform' subdomain, as in the tutorial's hi.platform.<domain> — i.e., the platform services cluster is among the spokes serving tenant apps despite the topology page placing tenant applications on workload clusters.
The 'minimum deploy path' excludes platform secrets, databases, custom domains, and update/rollback; it ends at Synced/Healthy plus one HTTP 200 over verified TLS from the published hostname.

The verification kubectl commands are executed with operator-granted read credentials (possibly by the operator alongside the tenant), since no self-service access path is shipped; the scenario treats this as an environmental prerequisite rather than a tenant capability.

A reasonable scenario timeout is ~10-15 minutes end-to-end (merge to HTTP 200), extrapolated from 'within a few minutes' for sync plus 'a couple of minutes' for first DNS; the docs give no hard bound.

blocked.at_step: Steps 5-7 (verification) when the actor is a pure self-service tenant
blocked.reason: No shipped path exists for a tenant human to obtain the kubectl access the verification steps require: onboarding lists 'No human kubectl access path' as a named gap and the only access guide (kubectl via directory group) is marked Stability: contract — 'do not automate against it until it flips to stable'. Proceeded by assuming operator-granted read access per the tutorial's prerequisite wording; without that grant, the tenant's only observable surface is the public URL in step 7.

notes: All pages on the core path (tutorial, deploy-an-application, onboard-a-tenant, expose-an-application, check-health-and-find-url) carry 'Stability: stable', defined on the About page as 'Shipped behavior, verified on a clean build of the platform' against which you may 'build executable scenarios and automation' — so this L1 is automatable by the docs' own contract, with the single exception of the tenant-access gap recorded in blocked[0]. The scenario's 'from a git repo' clause is satisfied by the platform monorepo model: 'If the tenant's chart lives in the platform repository — the common case today — nothing to do' (onboard-a-tenant); deploying from a separate tenant-owned repo would require the operator to allowlist it, since sources are 'exactly pinned repository URLs — no wildcards, mechanically enforced' and 'Deploying from any other repository is denied at admission' (reference/tenant-boundaries). Two tensions worth a human spot-check: (1) the topology explanation says tenant applications run on workload-cluster spokes while the stable tutorial/how-to examples land on the 'platform' subdomain and the deployment unit targets every spoke — mechanically consistent but thin guidance on placement (missing_facts 5-6); (2) the tutorial page reportedly says 'create platform-services/hi/ with four files' while five files (Chart.yaml, values.yaml, deployment/service/ingress templates) appear — possibly a doc nit, but all quotes here were extracted via a summarizing fetch tool and exact wording should be verified against the live pages before filing. ArgoCD's web UI is documented as requiring operator-level access, so kubectl (or the public URL) is the tenant's only stable verification surface.
